readings.title: Buckingham Palace
readings.challenge: Hear the same two lines come back in every stanza and listen for what changes.
readings.focus: A child’s questions and a nanny’s down-to-earth answers make a royal outing funny.
readings.context: From A. A. Milne’s When We Were Very Young (1924), poems written for and about his small son, Christopher Robin. Buckingham Palace is the King’s home in London, where soldiers called guards take turns on duty: the “changing of the guard.” Alice was Christopher Robin’s nanny. A sentry-box is a little hut for a guard; a hundred pounds was a great deal of money.

excerpt.locator: “Buckingham Palace,” the whole poem; opens “They’re changing guard at Buckingham Palace— Christopher Robin went down with Alice.…”; closes “…think the King knows all about me?” “Sure to, dear, but it’s time for tea,” Says Alice.”.

questions.prompt: Which two lines begin every stanza? Say them together the next time through.
facilitatorNotes: “They’re changing guard at Buckingham Palace— / Christopher Robin went down with Alice.” The repeat sounds like marching, and like a child who keeps going back to the same exciting place.
evidence: They’re changing guard at Buckingham Palace—

questions.prompt: Does Christopher Robin ever see the King? What do they see instead?
facilitatorNotes: No. They see a guard in a sentry-box and a face at a window, but “it wasn’t the King’s.” The poem is about waiting for someone who never comes.
evidence: We looked for the King, but he never came.
A face looked out, but it wasn’t the King’s.

questions.prompt: What kind of things does Alice say about soldiers and kings? Are they grand or ordinary?
facilitatorNotes: Ordinary: socks, hard work, signing papers, not wanting the job. She brings the palace down to everyday size. Some children may hear her as wise, others as not very interested.
evidence: One of the sergeants looks after their socks
I wouldn’t be King for a hundred pounds

questions.prompt: In the last stanza Christopher Robin asks, “Do you think the King knows all about me?” Why do you think he asks? What does Alice’s answer show?
facilitatorNotes: He wants to matter to the important man he came to see. Alice says “Sure to, dear” kindly, then changes the subject to tea. Children may feel she is loving, or that she is not really listening; both fit.
evidence: Do you think the King knows all about me?
Sure to, dear, but it’s time for tea

readings.title: The Christening
readings.challenge: Listen for a made-up word that rhymes, and for the reason given for each name.
readings.focus: Choosing a name for a pet, and the reason the last name wins.
readings.context: From A. A. Milne’s When We Were Very Young (1924), poems written for and about his small son, Christopher Robin. A christening is a ceremony where a baby is given a name. A dormouse is a small mouse-like animal with a long, furry tail. “’Cos” is a short way of saying “because.”

excerpt.locator: “The Christening,” the whole poem; opens “What shall I call My dear little dormouse? His eyes are small, But his tail is…”; closes “But I think I shall call him Jim, ’Cos I am so fond of him.”.

questions.prompt: The poem says the dormouse’s tail is “e-nor-mouse.” What real word is hiding in it, and why is it funny?
facilitatorNotes: Enormous, bent to rhyme with dormouse. Read it slowly in three parts as the poem writes it.
evidence: But his tail is e-nor-mouse.

questions.prompt: Name the three “Terrible” names. What reason goes with each?
facilitatorNotes: John and Jack because the tail goes on and on; James because the dormouse likes being called names. Notice how the lines for John go “on— / And on— / And on,” like the tail.
evidence: ’Cos his tail goes on—
’Cos he says he likes me calling him names

questions.prompt: Why does the child choose Jim in the end? How is that reason different from the others?
facilitatorNotes: “’Cos I am so fond of him.” The other names were about the tail or a game; the last is about love. Some children may prefer Terrible Jack; ask for their reason too.
evidence: But I think I shall call him Jim,
’Cos I am so fond of him.

readings.title: The Four Friends
readings.challenge: Keep four characters straight and notice which one the poem keeps coming back to.
readings.focus: Three big, noisy animals and one tiny snail who goes on a journey nobody notices.
readings.context: From A. A. Milne’s When We Were Very Young (1924), poems written for and about his small son, Christopher Robin. A stall, a manger and a pen are places where animals are kept. A huffle is a little puff of breath. A rumpus is a loud, wild noise. A compass is a tool that shows which way is north.

excerpt.locator: “The Four Friends,” the whole poem; opens “Ernest was an elephant, a great big fellow, Leonard was a lion with a six-foot tail,…”; closes “…new tail, George was a goat, as I think I have mentioned, But James was only a snail.”.

questions.prompt: Who are the four friends, and what is each one?
facilitatorNotes: Ernest the elephant, Leonard the lion, George the goat, and James the snail. Ask which one is smallest.
evidence: Ernest was an elephant, a great big fellow,
And James was a very small snail.

questions.prompt: What happens when the snail makes his noise, “the huffle of a snail in danger”?
facilitatorNotes: Nobody hears him at all: the elephant and lion are far too loud. Ask the child to make a huffle.
evidence: And nobody heard him at all.

questions.prompt: James “reached the end of his brick.” Is that a big journey or a small one?
facilitatorNotes: For a snail it is a whole journey, with a compass. The poem takes his small trip as seriously as the elephant’s noise. Children may find it funny or brave; both fit.
evidence: James went a journey with the goat’s new compass
And he reached the end of his brick.

questions.prompt: The last line says “But James was only a snail.” What does “only” make you feel about James?
facilitatorNotes: It sounds like he matters less; yet the poem has followed him the whole way. Some children will feel sorry for him, others will say he was the hero.
evidence: But James was only a snail.

readings.title: Lines and Squares
readings.challenge: Tell what is real in the street from what the child imagines.
readings.focus: A pavement game becomes a world of hungry bears.
readings.context: From A. A. Milne’s When We Were Very Young (1924), poems written for and about his small son, Christopher Robin. London pavements are made of square stones with lines between them. A lair is a wild animal’s den. “Portant” is the child’s way of saying “important.”

excerpt.locator: “Lines and Squares,” the whole poem; opens “Whenever I walk in a London street, I’m ever so careful to watch my feet; And I keep in…”; closes “…And it’s ever so jolly to call out, “Bears, Just watch me walking in all the squares!””.

questions.prompt: What is the rule of the child’s game?
facilitatorNotes: Walk only in the squares and never step on a line. Try it on a floor with tiles or boards.
evidence: And I keep in the squares,

questions.prompt: What will happen to “the sillies who tread on the lines,” according to the poem?
facilitatorNotes: Bears waiting at the corners will eat them. The child invents the danger that makes the game exciting.
evidence: Who wait at the corners all ready to eat

questions.prompt: What do the bigger bears pretend? Why might they pretend that?
facilitatorNotes: That they only came to look for a friend, and that nobody cares how you walk; they want you to stop being careful. Some children may say the child is trying to trick himself into stepping on a line.
evidence: That they came round the corner to look for a friend;

questions.prompt: Is the child frightened of the bears, or enjoying them? Find a line that shows it.
facilitatorNotes: Mostly enjoying: “it’s ever so jolly to call out.” He is showing off to the bears. A child who hears a little fear too can point to “It’s ever so portant how you walk.”
evidence: And it’s ever so jolly to call out, “Bears,
It’s ever so portant how you walk.

readings.title: Brownie
readings.challenge: Notice the lines in brackets and who speaks them.
readings.focus: A child half-believes in a hidden creature, and the grown-up plays along.
readings.context: From A. A. Milne’s When We Were Very Young (1924), poems written for and about his small son, Christopher Robin. A brownie is a small, helpful fairy creature from old stories that hides in houses. Nanny is the woman who looks after the child.

excerpt.locator: “Brownie,” the whole poem; opens “In a corner of the bedroom is a great big curtain, Someone lives behind it, but I don’t…”; closes “…They wriggle off at once because they’re all so tickly. (Nanny says they’re tickly too.)”.

questions.prompt: Where does the Brownie live?
facilitatorNotes: Behind the big curtain in a corner of the bedroom.
evidence: In a corner of the bedroom is a great big curtain,

questions.prompt: Why has the child never seen the Brownie properly?
facilitatorNotes: He goes “so quickly” and wriggles off, because Brownies are tickly. The poem gives a reason that also explains why there is nothing there.
evidence: Brownies never wait to say, “How do you do?”
They wriggle off at once because they’re all so tickly.

questions.prompt: Read the two lines in brackets again. What is Nanny doing?
facilitatorNotes: Agreeing with the child, or playing along: she “isn’t certain, too,” and says they’re tickly too. Some children may think Nanny really believes; others that she is being kind. Both can be argued.
evidence: (Nanny isn’t certain, too.)
(Nanny says they’re tickly too.)

readings.title: Independence
readings.challenge: Hear how a repeated phrase sounds like a child stamping a foot.
readings.focus: A small child is tired of being looked after.
readings.context: From A. A. Milne’s When We Were Very Young (1924), poems written for and about his small son, Christopher Robin. Independence means being able to do things by yourself. The words in quotation marks are things grown-ups say.

excerpt.locator: “Independence,” the whole poem; opens “I never did, I never did, I never did like “Now take care, dear!” I never did, I never…”; closes “…did think much of “Not up there, dear!” It’s no good saying it. They don’t understand.”.

questions.prompt: What three things do grown-ups say that the child doesn’t like?
facilitatorNotes: “Now take care, dear!”, “Hold-my-hand,” and “Not up there, dear!” Let the child say them in a grown-up voice.
evidence: I never did, I never did, I never did like “Now take care, dear!”

questions.prompt: Why does the poem say “I never did” three times in every line?
facilitatorNotes: It sounds like a child stamping and insisting, getting crosser each time. Read one line quietly and one loudly; which fits better?
evidence: I never did, I never did, I never did want “Hold-my-hand”;

questions.prompt: Who are “They” in the last line? Are they right not to understand?
facilitatorNotes: The grown-ups. The child thinks they cannot see he is big enough. Some children will side with the child; others will say grown-ups keep you safe. The title gives the child’s side its name.
evidence: It’s no good saying it. They don’t understand.

readings.title: Nursery Chairs
readings.challenge: Keep track of four chairs and the four different games they become.
readings.focus: Pretend play turns ordinary chairs into places, and the last question turns back to the child himself.
readings.context: From A. A. Milne’s When We Were Very Young (1924), poems written for and about his small son, Christopher Robin. A nursery was a child’s playroom. The Amazon is a great river in South America. A high chair is a tall chair for a little child at the table. “Round-the-World” is a sailor’s joke name for a place.
readings.contentNote: The first chair’s game imagines the Amazon’s Indigenous people, called “Indians” in the poem, as a band who obey the boy. This is a 1924 English child’s idea of adventure, not a true picture of anyone’s life.

excerpt.locator: “Nursery Chairs,” the whole poem with its four chair-poems; opens “One of the chairs is South America, One of the chairs is a ship at sea, One is a cage for…”; closes “…out in my ship to sea? Or get in my cage and be lions and tigers? Or—shall I be only Me?”.

questions.prompt: Name the four chairs and what each one becomes.
facilitatorNotes: South America, a lion’s cage, a ship at sea, and a chair where he pretends to be a baby of three. Point to a real chair and choose one.
evidence: One of the chairs is South America,
One is a cage for a great big lion,

questions.prompt: In the lion’s cage, the child frightens Nanny, then what does he do?
facilitatorNotes: He holds her tight and tells her not to be frightened. He is both the scary lion and the comforter. Ask why he might like being both.
evidence: Tell her not to be so frightened—

questions.prompt: In the first chair the boy only has to wave his hand, and the people “always understand.” Why might he like being in charge in this game?
facilitatorNotes: In pretend, he is in charge and everyone obeys. Some children may say it is unfair to the people in the game; that is worth talking about too, using the content note.
evidence: I simply wave my hand.
They always understand.

questions.prompt: The fourth chair is a real high chair, and he pretends to be “a baby of three.” Why is that funny? What is his last question?
facilitatorNotes: He is already a small child, so pretending to be a baby is a joke. The last question asks whether to play a game or “be only Me.” Children may say being Me is the best choice, or the dullest.
evidence: And that I am a baby of three.
Or—shall I be only Me?

readings.title: Market Square
readings.challenge: Follow the child’s money and the stalls he visits, and notice the surprise at the end.
readings.focus: A search through the market fails, and what he wanted turns up free on the common.
readings.context: From A. A. Milne’s When We Were Very Young (1924), poems written for and about his small son, Christopher Robin. A penny, tuppence (two pence) and a sixpence were English coins. Lavender is a sweet-smelling flower; mackerel is a fish. A common is open grassy land anyone may walk on. The stall-keepers’ calls are in brackets.

excerpt.locator: “Market Square,” the whole poem; opens “I had a penny, A bright new penny, I took my penny To the market square. I wanted a…”; closes “…the people who sell sweet lavender, ’Cos they haven’t got a rabbit, not anywhere there!”.

questions.prompt: What does the child want, and how much money does he have each time?
facilitatorNotes: A rabbit. First a penny, then two pennies, then a sixpence, then nothing. Count them up together.
evidence: I wanted a rabbit,
I found a sixpence,

questions.prompt: What do the stalls sell instead? How does the child answer each seller?
facilitatorNotes: Lavender, mackerel and saucepans. Each time he asks for a rabbit with a reason: he doesn’t want lavender, doesn’t like mackerel, and they already have two saucepans.
evidence: “Have you got a rabbit, ’cos I don’t want lavender?”
“Could I have a rabbit, ’cos we’ve got two saucepans?”

questions.prompt: When he has “nuffin’,” where does he go, and what does he find?
facilitatorNotes: The common, where he sees little rabbits everywhere: they were never for sale, and they cost nothing.
evidence: I had nuffin’,
And I saw little rabbits

questions.prompt: Why is he “sorry for the people” at the end? Is he right?
facilitatorNotes: He thinks they are missing the best thing because they have no rabbit. It is a child’s idea of what matters; the sellers may not mind at all. Some children will say he has learned that the best things are free.
evidence: So I’m sorry for the people who sell fine saucepans,

readings.title: Disobedience
readings.challenge: Notice who is supposed to obey whom, and hear how the poem changes in the last stanza.
readings.focus: A three-year-old in charge of his mother turns the usual rules upside down.
readings.context: From A. A. Milne’s When We Were Very Young (1924), poems written for and about his small son, Christopher Robin. Disobedience is not doing what you are told. A gown is a long dress. To be mislaid is to be lost, as if put down in the wrong place. Forty shillings was a reward in English money. To consult is to ask someone first. In the last stanza, “C/o” stands for “care of” and the stars hide letters of a word.

excerpt.locator: “Disobedience,” the whole poem; opens “James James Morrison Morrison Weatherby George Dupree Took great Care of his Mother,…”; closes “…said he: “You-must-never-go-down-to-the-end-of-the-town-if-you-don’t-go-down-with ME!””.

questions.prompt: Who gives the orders in this poem: the mother or the child?
facilitatorNotes: James James, though he is only three. Usually a parent says “never go off without me”; here the child says it. That is the joke of the title.
evidence:
Took great
Care of his Mother,
Though he was only three.
“You must never go down to the end of the town, if you don’t go down with me.”

questions.prompt: What does King John’s notice say about James’s mother?
facilitatorNotes: Lost, stolen or strayed; last seen wandering; forty shillings reward. It reads like a notice for a lost pet. Read it in a loud town-crier voice.
evidence: SEEMS TO HAVE BEEN MISLAID.

questions.prompt: The poem says “Now then, very softly.” How does the last stanza look and sound different?
facilitatorNotes: It is in short letters and stars, like a whispered secret or a code: J.J. for James James and M***** for Mother. Read it softly, as the poem asks, then the last line loudly.
evidence: (Now then, very softly)
C/o his M*****

questions.prompt: James’s mother “hasn’t been heard of since.” Is this sad, or funny, or both?
facilitatorNotes: The poem treats it as a joke, and everyone shrugs: “what can anyone do?” Some children will be worried about the mother; that feeling is fair too, and the silly whisper at the end tells us not to take it too hard.
evidence: Hasn’t been heard of since.
well, what can anyone do?

readings.title: The Three Foxes
readings.challenge: Listen for the extra “-es” endings that make the words silly.
readings.focus: Nonsense rhymes bend words to tell what three foxes did and didn’t do.
readings.context: From A. A. Milne’s When We Were Very Young (1924), poems written for and about his small son, Christopher Robin. A copse is a small wood. A fair has games and prizes; at a coconut shy you throw balls to knock coconuts off stands. Mince-pies and plum-puddings are English sweet foods.

excerpt.locator: “The Three Foxes,” the whole poem; opens “Once upon a time there were three little foxes Who didn’t wear stockings, and they didn’t…”; closes “…they didn’t wear trousies, And they didn’t wear stockings and they didn’t wear sockses.”.

questions.prompt: What don’t the three little foxes wear? What do they have instead?
facilitatorNotes: No stockings, socks, coats or trousers, but handkerchiefs in cardboard boxes.
evidence: Who didn’t wear stockings, and they didn’t wear sockses,
And they kept their handkerchiefs in cardboard boxes.

questions.prompt: Find the silly words. What are the real words, and why did the poet change them?
facilitatorNotes: Sockses, trousies, mouses, wopses, mince-pieses, shieses. He bends words to rhyme with “foxes” and “houses,” and it sounds like a small child talking. Let the child invent one.
evidence: And they played “Touch last” with a family of mouses.
They went out hunting, and they caught three wopses.

questions.prompt: The poet says “That’s all that I know.” How does the last stanza wrap up the poem?
facilitatorNotes: It goes back to the first things we heard: handkerchiefs, houses, no coats, no socks. The ending sounds like the beginning turned round. Some children will notice the order is changed.
evidence: That’s all that I know of the three little foxes
